title: A long-dead star
caption: The supernova remnant DEM L316A, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Rippling wisps of ionized gas spread across this Hubble image. They are DEM L316A, the remains of a long-dead star, lying some 160 000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the Milky Way's nearest galactic neighbors.

The star died in an especially bright and energetic kind of explosion called a Type Ia supernova. These are thought to happen when a white dwarf pulls more material from a close companion star than it can handle and becomes unstable. The result is a violent blast that hurls the star's outer layers into space at immense speeds.

As that expelled gas plows through the material between the stars, it heats it and ionizes it, meaning electrons are stripped from the atoms. This creates the faint glow recorded by Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged the remnant in visible and near-infrared light, including a hydrogen-alpha filter. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The glow is faint and partly in near-infrared light, so an eye would not see these wisps.

behind.people: See full credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, Y. Chu
behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The Large Magellanic Cloud is a satellite of the Milky Way and the fourth-largest galaxy in the Local Group. Hubble has imaged other supernova remnants there too, including SNR 0509 in 2010 and SNR 0519 in 2013.
alt: Rippling wisps of glowing gas from an exploded star.
